title: Tanzanian Cassava Leaves
community: Popular across mainland Tanzania and coastal regions
author: Mama Salima

heritage.origin: Tanzania mainland and coastal regions — a uniquely East African vegetable preparation
heritage.history: Kisamvu (cassava leaves) is one of Tanzania's most distinctive vegetable dishes — the leaves of the cassava plant, which most cuisines discard, are harvested, pounded or finely chopped, and cooked until completely tender in a peanut and coconut sauce. Rich in protein and vitamins, kisamvu has sustained Tanzanian communities for centuries and represents the zero-waste food philosophy of the East African kitchen.

desc: Tanzanian Kisamvu — young cassava leaves pounded or finely chopped and slow-cooked with peanuts, coconut milk, and spices until completely tender and richly flavoured. One of Tanzania's most distinctive and nutritious vegetables — the dish that uses what most kitchens discard.
longDesc: Kisamvu is one of the most nutritionally complete vegetable dishes in East Africa — the cassava leaves are high in protein, the peanuts add fat and more protein, and the coconut milk adds MCTs. Together they produce a dish of extraordinary nutritional density from ingredients that are entirely free or very inexpensive.
ingredients: 400g fresh young cassava leaves — washed and finely chopped or pounded
equipment: Mortar or food processor for leaves
steps: Pound leaves in a mortar or pulse in a food processor until very finely broken down.
Blanch pounded leaves in boiling water for 10 minutes. Drain.
Heat oil. Cook onions until golden.
Add garlic, ginger, tomatoes, and spices. Cook 6 minutes.
Add blanched leaves. Stir to combine.
Mix groundnut paste with ½ cup warm water until smooth. Add to pot.
Add coconut milk and remaining water.
Simmer covered 30—35 minutes until completely tender and sauce is thick.
chefTips: Very young, tender leaves only — mature leaves are tough even after long cooking.
Pounding breaks down the fibrous leaf structure — essential for the right texture.
Blanching removes some of the naturally occurring compounds that require long cooking.
The groundnut paste must be mixed with warm water first — prevents lumping.
cookingScience: Cassava leaves contain linamarin (same as the root) which must be broken down through a combination of cell rupture (pounding) and heat (cooking). Pounding ruptures cell walls releasing the enzyme linamarase which breaks down linamarin; the subsequent blanching and long cooking ensures complete neutralisation.
sustainabilityTips: Cassava leaves are free — they are removed when cassava is grown for the root and would otherwise be discarded. Zero cost, maximum nutrition.
healthBenefits: Very high protein for a leaf vegetable.
Rich in calcium, iron, and vitamins A and C.
Peanuts add protein and healthy fats.
culturalNote: Kisamvu represents Tanzania's zero-waste food wisdom — the cassava leaf that would be discarded in most cuisines is transformed into one of the country's most nutritious and beloved vegetable dishes.
